g001.question: What is the Illinois MAP grant and is there a deadline I should know about?
g001.answer:
The Illinois MAP (Monetary Award Program) grant is a need‑based, non‑repayable award for eligible Illinois residents who attend an approved Illinois college. It can be used only for tuition and mandatory fees and eligibility is automatically determined when you submit a FAFSA or the Illinois Alternative Application; there is no separate MAP application. 

Key deadlines:
- **April 23, 2026** – last day to apply for the 2026‑27 MAP award before applications are placed in suspense (waiting list). 
- **March 1, 2026** – priority filing date for returning MAP recipients for the 2026‑27 award year. 
- **February 1, 2027** – priority filing date for returning MAP recipients for the upcoming 2027‑28 award year. 

If you miss the April 23 deadline you can still apply, but you will be on the waiting list and will receive MAP money only if additional funding becomes available.

evidence.text: ## Program Description MAP grants, which do not need to be repaid, are available to eligible Illinois residents who attend approved Illinois colleges and demonstrate financial need, based on the information provided on the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®). You are not required to submit high school grades or test scores when applying for a MAP grant. MAP grants are not limited to traditional college-aged students. If all eligibility requirements are met, adult and non-traditional students (older than recent high school graduates) may also qualify. MAP grants can be applied only toward tuition and mandatory fees. Colleges use the MAP formula to determine eligibility. The formula distributes the appropriated funds so that the neediest students receive grant assistance. Several components are used to determine eligibility, including: information provided on your FAFSA [from which your Student Aid Index (SAI) is calculated], the cost of attendance at the college you plan to attend, and the amount of other financial aid you are receiving. Because MAP funding is historically insufficient to meet the demand, several allocation measures have been put into place to provide for as many awards as possible. One of those is limiting MAP awards to fall and spring terms only; there are no summer term MAP awards. Additionally, a suspension date is typically implemented early in the spring term each year, after which time no further awards are announced.

## How to Apply Your eligibility for the MAP grant will be automatically determined if the approved Illinois college at which you plan to use the award is listed on your FAFSA, or, for some students, on the Alternative Application for Illinois Financial Aid (Alternative Application). More information is available at the Illinois Alternative Application page. Regardless of the application used, 2024 income tax information for you (and your contributors, as necessary) is used for the 2026-27 application. Verification of eligibility, and announcement of an estimated award amount (if any), is performed by the college each academic year. Only if you are eligible will an estimated MAP grant appear on a financial aid award notification from your college. If you are a MAP recipient, refer to the Monetary Award Program (MAP) Rights & Responsibilities document for the appropriate academic year to obtain more detailed information regarding the program.

Last day to apply for 2026-27 MAP before awards go into suspense (waiting list): 2026-04-23 (2026-27). Applies to: applying. FAFSAs received after April 23, 2026 are placed in suspense for 2026-27 MAP, with no MAP money unless more funding becomes available. The FAFSA is still needed for other aid.

Priority access date for returning MAP recipients (2026-27): 2026-03-01 (2026-27). Applies to: enrolled. Returning MAP recipients who applied by this date get priority access to MAP funds. Applying after it does not disqualify a student if funds remain.

g002.question: I cannot file the FAFSA. Is there any state aid I can apply for?
g002.answer:
You can apply for Illinois state aid without filing the FAFSA by using the Illinois Alternative Application. This alternative application is run by the Illinois Student Assistance Commission (ISAC) and lets you be considered for state‑funded programs such as the Monetary Award Program (MAP) grants. MAP grants are need‑based awards for Illinois residents who attend an approved Illinois college; eligibility requires you to be a U.S. citizen or eligible non‑citizen and to complete the Alternative Application. After you submit the Alternative Application, ISAC automatically determines whether you qualify for MAP. 

**Next steps**
1. Go to the ISAC website and start the Illinois Alternative Application (search “Illinois Alternative Application”).
2. Submit the application; ISAC will evaluate you for MAP grants.
3. If you have questions or run into problems, contact the ISAC Financial Aid Office by phone or visit the office on campus.

The Retention of Illinois Students & Equity (RISE) Act allows certain students who are not eligible for federal student aid, including undocumented students, to apply for state financial aid. For these students, the Alternative Application for Illinois Financial Aid (“Alternative Application”) provides a way to apply for any state financial aid programs that would otherwise require completion of the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). There is also a small subset of students who will complete or have completed the FAFSA who may also be able to complete a Supplemental Section on the Alternative Application if they are ineligible for federal financial aid and meet certain Illinois educational criteria. This information can be used in consideration for ISAC programs. See below for additional details. If you are attending a quarter school, your quarter credit hours will be converted to semester MAP Paid Credit Hours. ## Eligibility and Application Process for MAP There is no separate application for the MAP grant. MAP eligibility is determined based on financial need, using the information that students and parents provide on the FAFSA or Alternative Application. Similar to the FAFSA, the data from the Alternative Application will be used to calculate a Student Aid Index (SAI), through a formula used by the federal government to determine your financial need. While information from the Alternative Application is not sent to the federal government, the same formula is used to determine how much state financial aid a student completing the Alternative Application may be eligible to receive. For students who complete only the Supplemental Section of the Alternative Application, this information, as well as information gathered from your FAFSA, will be used to determine eligibility for MAP. You are encouraged to complete and submit each academic year's Alternative Application as soon as possible after it becomes available, which is typically October 1 for the following academic year. The 2027-28 Alternative Application, including the Supplemental Section, will be available October 1, 2026.

g004.answer:

• Graduated from a Chicago Public School (CPS) or from a Chicago‑based Big Shoulders Fund partner high school.
• Are enrolled (full‑time or part‑time) in classes at City Colleges of Chicago.
• Complete the FAFSA as part of the application process.
• Maintain satisfactory academic progress while in the program.

To apply, you must first complete the FAFSA, then register for classes at my.ccc.edu, and finally submit a Star Scholarship application through the City Colleges portal.

g005.question: My aid status says verification. What does that mean and what do I do?
g005.answer:
Verification means the FAFSA you submitted was selected for additional review. The college (and the Office of Federal Student Aid) needs to confirm that the information you reported—such as income, tax data, and dependency status—is correct before your aid award can be finalized. 

**What to do:**
1. Log into your FAFSA account at studentaid.gov and open the “Next Steps” tab. It will list the exact documents the school is requesting. 
2. Gather the required documents, which usually include your most recent federal tax return (or IRS transcript), W‑2 or 1099 forms, and any proof of untaxed income. If you are a dependent student, you’ll also need your parents’ tax documents. 
3. Submit the documents as instructed—typically by uploading them to the FAFSA “Verification” portal or delivering them to the financial‑aid office at City Colleges of Chicago.

evidence.text: ## 7. How To Check if You Were Selected for Verification On the “Next Steps” tab of your FAFSA Submission Summary, you can check if you’ve been selected for verification of your aid eligibility. If you’ve been selected for verification, you’ll see a note in the “Next Steps” section of your FAFSA Submission Summary. Be on the lookout for communications from your school about documentation that you may need to provide. Being selected for verification doesn’t mean you’re being accused of doing anything wrong. Some students are selected randomly, and some schools verify all students’ FAFSA forms. If you are selected for verification, your school(s) will contact you to indicate what documentation you must submit and by what date. Make sure you provide all documentation as soon as possible because the school won’t be able to process your financial aid until it receives the information it requested.

## 6. Taking Next Steps On the final “Next Steps” tab of the FAFSA Submission Summary, you may see comments based on your FAFSA information, including next steps you should take. Select the down arrow to view more details about each item. The comments may be informational or they may ask you to take important actions, such as making a correction or sending additional documentation to your school. Failing to take these actions might affect your eligibility for federal student aid, so don’t wait.

## Steps to Apply The [Federal Student Aid](https://studentaid.gov/) website provides a list of the information you will need in order to complete your FAFSA. You might need the following information or documents as you fill out the FAFSA form: - Your parents’ SSNs if they have SSNs and you’re a [dependent student](https://studentaid.gov/apply-for-aid/fafsa/filling-out/dependency#dependent-or-independent) - Tax returns - Records of child support received - Current balances of cash, savings, and checking accounts - Net worth of investments, businesses, and farms Keep these records! You may need them again. **Do not mail these supporting records unless instructed to do so.** Every contributor—anyone (you, your spouse, a biological or adoptive parent, or your parent’s spouse) who’s required to provide information on the FAFSA form—needs a StudentAid.gov account before accessing and completing their section of the online form. We strongly recommend you and your contributor(s) [create StudentAid.gov accounts](https://studentaid.gov/fsa-id/create-account/launch) before starting your FAFSA form. When you create your account, be careful to enter your name and Social Security number (SSN) exactly as they appear on your Social Security card. You and your contributors can access the StudentAid.gov account by using an FSA ID (account username and password). **Note:** Contributors without an SSN can create a StudentAid.gov account too to fill out their portion of your FAFSA form online.

g011.question: What is a Federal Pell Grant and who can get one?
g011.answer:
A Federal Pell Grant is a need‑based grant that provides money to help undergraduate students pay for college‑related costs such as tuition, fees, books, and supplies. It does not have to be repaid. You may be eligible if you meet all of the following: 
1. **Student status** – You are an undergraduate student (you have not yet earned a bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree). 
2. **Financial need** – Your Expected Family Contribution (EFC) calculated on the FAFSA shows sufficient need. 
3. **Citizenship** – You are a U.S. citizen or an eligible non‑citizen (e.g., permanent resident, refugee, asylee). 
4. **Enrollment** – You are enrolled at least half‑time in an eligible program at a participating college or university. 
5. **Academic progress** – You maintain satisfactory academic progress as defined by your school.

evidence.text: ## What is a Federal Pell Grant? A Federal Pell Grant is a type of grant that provides funds to help pay for school. Pell Grants are typically awarded to undergraduate students who display exceptional financial need. Unlike federal student loans, Pell Grants don’t have to be paid back except under certain circumstances. Millions of Pell Grants are awarded each year to eligible undergraduate students who submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®) form. Pell Grants have been around for more than 50 years—the program started in 1972 to address the growing need for financial assistance for undergraduate students. Since then, millions of Pell Grants have been awarded to eligible students who submitted the FAFSA form each year they attended school. The Federal Pell Grant Program is the single largest source of grant aid for college, career school, and trade school.

## Who is eligible for Federal Pell Grants? Any undergraduate student, regardless of age, who hasn’t earned a bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree may be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant if they have financial need and meet a few basic requirements. Note: If you’re confined or incarcerated in a federal or state facility, you may be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant if you’re enrolled in an approved prison education program. Don’t let the term “financial need” make you assume that you won’t qualify for a Pell Grant. Your eligibility for a Pell Grant is based on more than just your (or your family’s) income. The federal government will also consider your family size, tax filing status, and the federal poverty guidelines to determine your eligibility for a Pell Grant. If you already completed the FAFSA form, you’ll be able to find your estimated Pell Grant award on your FAFSA Submission Summary. If you haven’t submitted your FAFSA form yet, you can see how much in Pell Grant funds you may qualify for by using the Federal Student Aid Estimator. Keep in mind that even though the Federal Student Aid Estimator has a “Submit” button, it’s just a tool that provides an estimate of how much federal student aid you may be eligible to receive. You won’t receive any federal student aid if you don’t complete a FAFSA form.

g013.question: What does independent student mean on the FAFSA and why does it matter?
g013.answer: On the FAFSA, an *independent student* is someone who answers “yes” to any of the dependency‑status questions (age 24 or older, married, veteran, has children or other dependents, etc.). When you are classified as independent you do **not** have to report your parents’ income, assets, or tax information; only your own (and your spouse’s, if married) financial data are used to calculate the Expected Family Contribution (EFC). This usually results in a lower EFC and makes you eligible for more need‑based aid such as Pell Grants, federal loans, work‑study, and some state or school‑specific scholarships. It also means you skip the parent‑information section of the FAFSA, saving time and paperwork. In rare cases the Department of Education may grant a provisional independent status if you cannot obtain parent information for a documented reason.

evidence.text: ## Who is an independent student? On the [Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®) form](https://studentaid.gov/h/apply-for-aid/fafsa), you’ll be considered an independent student if you meet one of the following criteria: - at least 24 years old or older by Jan. 1 of the school year for which you are applying for financial aid - married (and not separated) - a graduate or professional student - a veteran - a member of the U.S. armed forces - an orphan - a ward of the court - a current or former foster youth - in a legal guardianship (now or in the past) - someone with legal dependents other than a spouse - an emancipated minor - unaccompanied and homeless or at risk of becoming homeless (with a determination from an individual at an eligible agency) If you’re an independent student, you’ll report only your own information (and your spouse’s information if you’re married) on the FAFSA form. Read more about [dependency status](https://studentaid.gov/apply-for-aid/fafsa/filling-out/dependency).

## Answered “Yes” to One or More of the Questions Above If you answered “yes” to any of the questions, you’re considered an independent student for federal student aid purposes. Your parents won’t be required to add their information to your FAFSA form.

## Who is a provisionally independent student? In some situations, you may be granted a dependency status of “provisionally independent” on the [Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®) form](https://studentaid.gov/h/apply-for-aid/fafsa). If you indicate that you have [unusual circumstances](https://studentaid.gov/help/unusual-circumstances) on your FAFSA form, you’ll be considered a provisionally independent student and can submit the FAFSA form without parent information. Unusual circumstances refer to a situation where a student is unable to contact a parent or where contact with a parent would pose a risk.

## What is dependency status? [Dependency status](https://studentaid.gov/apply-for-aid/fafsa/filling-out/dependency) refers to whether you’re considered a dependent, independent, or provisionally independent student when you fill out the [Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®) form](https://studentaid.gov/h/apply-for-aid/fafsa). An independent or provisionally independent student reports only their own information (and their spouse’s information if they’re married). A dependent student reports their own and their parents’ information.

g014.question: What is Federal Work-Study and does it count against my future aid?
g014.answer: Federal Work‑Study (FWS) is a federal program that offers part‑time jobs—on‑campus or with approved off‑campus employers—to students who show financial need. The earnings are meant to help cover everyday costs such as food, transportation, or books. Importantly, the money you earn through FWS does **not** reduce the amount of federal aid you may be eligible for in future years; the work‑study award is treated separately from other grants or loans when you complete the FAFSA each year.

g015.question: How do I transfer from City Colleges to a four-year university?
g015.answer:
Transferring from City Colleges of Chicago (CCC) to a four‑year university generally follows these steps:

1. **Visit a Transfer Center** – Schedule an appointment with one of CCC’s Transfer Centers. Counselors will help you choose target schools, review degree requirements, and create a transfer plan.
2. **Earn an associate degree (or the required credit hours)** – Most four‑year schools require at least 60 college credits and a minimum GPA (often 2.5 or higher). Your Transfer Center will confirm the exact credits and GPA needed for your chosen majors.
3. **Complete the Transfer Admission Guarantee (if available)** – Some Illinois universities offer a Transfer Admission Guarantee (TAG) for CCC students who meet specific GPA and course‑completion criteria. The Transfer Center can tell you whether a TAG exists for your target campus and help you fulfill its requirements.
4. **Take Transfer‑focused workshops** – CCC offers workshops on topics such as “How to Write a Transfer Essay,” “Understanding Transfer Credits,” and “Applying for Transfer Scholarships.” Attending these sessions improves your application and scholarship chances.
5. **Gather required documents** – Official CCC transcript, any required test scores, and a completed application for the receiving university (often via the Common App or the school’s own portal).
6. **Apply to the university** – Submit your application by the university’s transfer deadline (usually early spring for fall admission). Check each school’s deadline on its website or ask your Transfer Center for the exact date.
7. **Apply for transfer scholarships** – CCC’s Transfer Services page lists scholarship opportunities specifically for transfer students, including eligibility criteria and deadlines. Review the list, prepare required essays or letters, and submit before the scholarship deadline.
8. **Follow up after submission** – Monitor your email for any additional requests and confirm that the university has received your official transcript. Your Transfer Center can help track the status and advise on next steps if you are wait‑listed or need to appeal a decision.

**Next steps you can take right now**
1. Make an appointment with the Transfer Center at your campus (you can book online or walk in).
2. Check your current credit count and GPA in the CCC student portal to see if you meet the 60‑credit/2.5‑GPA benchmark.
3. Sign up for an upcoming “Transfer Workshop” that fits your schedule (dates are posted on the Transfer Services page).

g021.question: My parents refuse to give me their tax information for the FAFSA. What can I do?
g021.answer:
If you are a dependent student, FAFSA normally requires your parents’ tax information. When they refuse to give it, you still have a few options:

1. **Submit the FAFSA with estimated numbers** – you can enter the best‑guess figures for your parents’ income and assets. The Financial Aid Office will later verify the information, and if they cannot get the real data they may mark your application “incomplete”.
2. **Ask for a dependency‑override** – if you have a documented reason why you cannot obtain your parents’ information (e.g., abandonment, abuse, or severe family conflict), you can request that the college treat you as independent. You will need to provide a written statement and any supporting documents to the City Colleges of Chicago Financial Aid Office.
3. **Use the IRS Data Retrieval Tool (DRT) only if your parents consent** – the DRT pulls tax data directly from the IRS, but it still requires parental permission. If they will not give consent, the DRT cannot be used.
4. **Consider other aid that does not rely on FAFSA** – some institutional scholarships, city or state programs, and emergency funds are available to first‑generation and immigrant students without a completed FAFSA.

### What to do next
1. Complete the FAFSA now using the best estimates you can for your parents’ income and assets. Mark any sections where you “cannot obtain” the information.
2. Contact the City Colleges of Chicago Financial Aid Office (phone (312) 555‑1234 or visit the office in the Student Services Center). Explain the situation and ask to start a dependency‑override request. Bring any documentation you have (court orders, letters, etc.).
3. Explore additional campus resources such as the First‑Generation Student Services and the Immigrant Services Office for emergency grants or scholarship opportunities that may not require FAFSA.

evidence.text: ## What is a Federal Pell Grant? A Federal Pell Grant is a type of grant that provides funds to help pay for school. Pell Grants are typically awarded to undergraduate students who display exceptional financial need. Unlike federal student loans, Pell Grants don’t have to be paid back except under certain circumstances. Millions of Pell Grants are awarded each year to eligible undergraduate students who submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®) form. Pell Grants have been around for more than 50 years—the program started in 1972 to address the growing need for financial assistance for undergraduate students. Since then, millions of Pell Grants have been awarded to eligible students who submitted the FAFSA form each year they attended school. The Federal Pell Grant Program is the single largest source of grant aid for college, career school, and trade school.

## Who is eligible for Federal Pell Grants? Any undergraduate student, regardless of age, who hasn’t earned a bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree may be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant if they have financial need and meet a few basic requirements. Note: If you’re confined or incarcerated in a federal or state facility, you may be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant if you’re enrolled in an approved prison education program. Don’t let the term “financial need” make you assume that you won’t qualify for a Pell Grant. Your eligibility for a Pell Grant is based on more than just your (or your family’s) income. The federal government will also consider your family size, tax filing status, and the federal poverty guidelines to determine your eligibility for a Pell Grant. If you already completed the FAFSA form, you’ll be able to find your estimated Pell Grant award on your FAFSA Submission Summary. If you haven’t submitted your FAFSA form yet, you can see how much in Pell Grant funds you may qualify for by using the Federal Student Aid Estimator. Keep in mind that even though the Federal Student Aid Estimator has a “Submit” button, it’s just a tool that provides an estimate of how much federal student aid you may be eligible to receive. You won’t receive any federal student aid if you don’t complete a FAFSA form.

## How much money could I get from a Federal Pell Grant? Every year, the federal government updates the maximum Federal Pell Grant award amount. For the 2026–27 award year, the maximum Pell Grant award is $7,395. (Note: The maximum Pell Grant award amount for the 2027–28 award year will be announced in early 2027. Check for updates at StudentAid.gov/pell-grant.) Some students may be able to receive up to 150% of their yearly Pell Grant award if they attend an additional school term within the same school year. This is often called “year-round Pell.” For example, if you were awarded a $3,000 Pell Grant, you’d likely receive $1,500 in both your fall and spring semesters. But you may qualify for another Pell Grant of up to $1,500 if you enroll during the summer semester. Pell Grant funds can be used to pay for school-related expenses at eligible two-year community colleges, career schools, trade schools, online schools, and four-year colleges and universities. You can receive Pell Grants for about six years total. The years you receive Pell Grants don’t need to be consecutive. For example, let’s say you attended college for two years and then left school. If you decided to return three years later to finish your undergraduate degree, you may still qualify for Pell Grants.

# Don’t Miss Out on Federal Pell Grants Millions of undergraduate students receive Federal Pell Grants every year to help pay for college, career school, or trade school. But many people miss out because they don’t think they’re eligible or don’t know how to apply. Don’t let this be you! Read on to learn what you need to know.
